acceptedAnswer.text: Ecommerce ROI is the return you get on the money you put into your store, expressed as a percentage. You take the net profit of a period, you divide it by everything that period cost you, and you multiply by 100. A ROI of 40% means every 100 spent came back as 140.

mainEntity.name: What is the ROI formula for ecommerce?

acceptedAnswer.text: ROI = ((revenue − total costs) / total costs) × 100. Total costs include the cost of goods sold, ad spend, platform and payment fees, shipping and any other operating cost tied to the period. Leave one of them out and the percentage flatters you.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between ROI and ROAS?

acceptedAnswer.text: ROAS divides revenue by ad spend, so it only judges advertising. ROI divides net profit by every cost you carry, so it judges the business. A campaign can post a healthy ROAS while the store behind it loses money on each order.

mainEntity.name: What is a good ROI for an ecommerce store?

acceptedAnswer.text: Above 15% is a workable return once ads are in the mix, and above 40% is strong. Below zero you are paying to sell. The right target depends on your channel and your margin: a store selling on paid social lives in a very different range from one selling through email and search.

mainEntity.name: What is a good ROAS for dropshipping?

acceptedAnswer.text: The honest answer is that there is no universal number, only your break-even ROAS. Divide your average order value by your gross margin per order and you get the ROAS you must beat. A store with a 35% margin needs roughly 2.9, a store with a 20% margin needs 5. Operators generally try to keep that break-even under 2, because above it every attempt to scale eats margin faster than it adds volume.

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate my break-even point?

acceptedAnswer.text: In period mode, break-even revenue equals your total costs: below that line you lose money, above it you keep the difference. In order mode, break-even is a number of orders: fixed costs and ad spend divided by the gross margin one order leaves you.

mainEntity.name: What costs should I include in my ROI calculation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cost of goods, shipping, platform and payment fees, ad spend, and the operating costs you would still pay if you sold nothing: apps, subscriptions, freelancers. Refunds and chargebacks belong there too, either as a cost line or as a return rate.

mainEntity.name: How do I find my COGS in Shopify?

acceptedAnswer.text: Open a product, then a variant, and read the cost per item field. Shopify aggregates it in Analytics under the cost of goods sold metric, and your supplier invoices give you the same figure. Add the inbound shipping your supplier charges you, it belongs to the product cost.

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate ROI per product?

acceptedAnswer.text: Switch the calculator to order mode. You enter the average order value, the product cost, the shipping and the fees for a single product, plus the volume you sold, and the ROI is computed on that product alone instead of the whole store.

mainEntity.name: Can I have a high ROAS and still lose money?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, and it is the most common way a store bleeds quietly. ROAS ignores the cost of the product, the shipping, the fees and the refunds. If those eat more than the margin left by the sale, the campaign looks profitable in the ads manager and the bank account still goes down.

mainEntity.name: How does product margin affect ROI?

acceptedAnswer.text: It sets the ceiling. Margin is what absorbs your advertising: two products sold at the same ROAS return very different ROI if one leaves 40% gross margin and the other 15%. Improving margin lifts every campaign you run afterwards, without touching the ads.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between gross profit and net profit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Gross profit is revenue minus the cost of goods, so it tells you what a sale leaves before you run the business. Net profit takes ads, fees, shipping and operating costs out too. Only net profit is money you can actually keep.

mainEntity.name: How often should I calculate my ecommerce ROI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Monthly for the store, and per product or per campaign whenever you are about to scale one. Tracking the same calculation over several periods is what makes a change readable: a price rise or a supplier switch shows up as a moving ROI, not as a feeling.

mainEntity.name: Does this calculator work for dropshipping?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. It was built around dropshipping economics: thin margins, ad-driven traffic and a product cost that moves with your supplier. It works just as well for a stocked store, since the cost lines are the same.
